traits.notes: Multiple leaves are damaged with small holes and irregular margins, likely from herbivory, but cause not inferred. Leaves are arranged in a whorled pattern around the apex, forming a rosette-like structure. Central inflorescence is visible with small, clustered, reddish-brown buds. All images show the same individual seedling from slightly different angles.

rag_matches.description:
Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 10. Maquira Aubl. By C.C. Berg. Trees or shrubs, dioecious. Leaves alternate, distichous on lateral branches; blade leathery, margins entire, pinnate-veined; stipules not completely amplexicaul, free. Inflorescences on spurs in the axils of the leaves, unisexual, discoid-capitate, involucrate. Staminate inflorescences often several together, pedunculate; flowers not covered by the inner involucral bracts before anthesis, numerous; perianth 4-parted to 4-divided; stamens 4; pistillode absent. Pistillate inflorescences subsessile; flowers numerous; perianth 4-lobed; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, tongue-shaped. Fruit-bearing perianth enlarged, fleshy, orange; fruits adnate to the perianth; seed large, without endosperm, cotyledons thick and equal. 4 spp. Tropical America.

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the Parque Nacional Carara], [in the Puriscal region (in the Parque Nacional La Cangreja)], [in the Parque Nacional Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica and Panama], [in Ecuador and Peru], [in Northeast Brazil].

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub 
3. Terminalia L., nom. cons. Buceras P. Browne, Bucida L. by C.A. Stace. Trees or shrubs, sometimes spiny. Leaves alternate or spirally arranged, without glandular trichomes. Inflorescences simple, expanded or rarely in condensed axillary spikes. Flowers bisexual or bisexual and staminate in the same inflorescence, actinomorphic; upper part of the hypanthium funnel-shaped to bell-shaped; sepals 5, somewhat short to very short; petals absent; stamens 10, exserted, anthers versatile; style free. Dry fruit, with (1-)2-5(-6) wings, either dry or succulent and ribbed to terete, sometimes with the upper part of the hypanthium and the calyx persistent on it. 150-200 spp. Pantropical, with 33 spp. in America, from the United States and Mexico to Argentina. In America, Terminalia is easily distinguished from Combretum by having leaves arranged in a spiral (not opposite), without glandular trichomes and by the absence of petals. Terminalia ivorensis A. Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs.

Locating an individual
Cantarrana, around the station.
Distribution
From Mexico to Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid wet forests on both slopes; 0-1,150 m.
Habit
Tree, 10-35 m tall.
Trunk
Cylindrical trunk, with slender, cylindrical, grayish twigs; small stipules attached to the petiole.
Bark
With smooth, grayish bark.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 2.5-12 x 0.8-5 cm, ovate to oblong, acuminate apex, rounded to cupped base, whitish or grayish on the underside, 5-9 pairs of secondary veins, entire margin; petioles 3-7 mm long.
Flowers
Greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5 mm long, with absent petals and 3-5 stamens. Inflorescences panicles, up to 16 cm long.
Fruits
Fruits drupes, 1.5-1.8 cm long, pear-shaped to ovoid, pink when ripe.
Diagnosis
Distinguished by its clearly bicolored leaves, the underside whitish to grayish and the thin blade with very fine reticulation. Also, by its pear-shaped fruits.
Habitat
Generally observed in forests on rolling terrain.
Phenology
Fruits observed in July.

Shrub or small tree, 1-4 m, moderately to densely covered with flexuous, hooked or feathery trichomes, hyaline, and moderately intermixed with tiny, oblong glands, on young twigs, petioles, primary veins raised on the undersides of leaves and inflorescences. Leaves 10—29(—39) X (6—)11-21.5 cm, broadly elliptical to elliptical-ovate, broadly rounded and obliquely cordate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, inconspicuously wavy-denticulate, glabrous on the adaxial surface, moderately covered on the abaxial surface with a mixture of simple, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes on the secondary and higher order veins, palmately 5-7-nerved. Inflorescences with bracteoles 0.5-1 mm, subulate, persistent. Flowers with pedicel 1.5-2.5 mm, 5-merous, the hypanthium sparsely covered with a mixture of star-shaped, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes; calyx with lobes 0.25-0.5 mm, wavy and apiculate, the external teeth ca. 0.25 mm, not projecting beyond the lobes, tuberculate; petals white or pale pink, 2.5—4(—5) X 1.5(—3) mm, obovate-oblong, glabrous; anthers yellow, subequal, 1.5-2 mm, oblong, bilocular, with a truncate to retuse pore, the connective without appendage; ovary ca. 3/4 inferior, 5-locular, apex sparsely glandular-pubescent, without a neck; style 3-4 mm, glabrous; stigma not expanded. Fruits black purple at maturity, 5-6 X 5-6 mm; seeds 0.5-0.75 mm, broadly deltoid in outline, rounded-angled, smooth, the raphe extended on all sides to form a swollen edge, like a wing. Very wet forest, riverbanks, 50-700 m; Caribbean slope. Cordillera de Talamanca, San Carlos Plain, Pacific slope, Northern Costeña Range (Fila Tinamastes), Southern Nicoya Peninsula, Parque Nacional Carara, regions of Puriscal and Golfo Dulce. Flowers April, July, August, November, December. Miconia simplex is recognized by its large leaves, broadly rounded to obliquely cordate at the base and shortly acuminate at the apex, the connective of the anthers without appendage, the ovary 5-locular, and the seeds with an inflated wing-like margin.

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the National Park Carara], [in the Puriscal region] (P.N. La Cangreja), [in the National Park Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica] and [in Panama], [in Ecuador] and [in Peru], [in Northern Brazil]. Trichilia tuberculata is distinguished by its densely verrucous fruits and restricted distribution in [Costa Rica] to very humid forest of the Pacific slope.
